Diagnosis begins with estimating probability based on a validated clinical decision rule (), then using a validated diagnostic algorithm integrating findings from D-dimer, lower extremity ultrasound, and CT scanning with intravenous contrast (ie, CT pulmonary angiography or CT-PA) (see ). A
Anticoagulation may begin in all patients strongly suspected of having PE without a high bleeding risk, before diagnostic testing is obtained. B

A direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) is the preferred therapy, due to slightly lower risk of major bleeding compared to warfarin. An exception is patients with antiphospholipid syndrome who should receive warfarin.A
Extended duration anticoagulation should be recommended for patients with an unprovoked PE and low to moderate bleeding risk (see ). A

background.definition: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a partial or total thromboembolic occlusion of the pulmonary arteries. PE has shared pathophysiology with deep vein thrombosis (DVT), (a thrombotic occlusion of the deep venous system of the legs), and together, along with superficial venous thrombosis, comprise the spectrum of venous thromboembolism (VTE).

list.listitem: Reportedly 117 episodes per 100,000 persons per year, with approximately one third leading to death.
Fewer than 5 episodes per 100,000 per year in persons younger than 15 years; approximately 500 per 100,000 per year in persons 80 years or older.
PE accounts for approximately 10% of hospital deaths and is the most common preventable cause of death among hospitalized patients in the United States.
Most patients will have one or more identified risk factors (see ); these risk factors are generally cumulative.

Oral contraceptives are the most important cause of thrombosis in young women, especially drospirenone-containing OCs (rate ratio for venous or arterial thrombosis 4.0-6.3 vs. 1.0-3.3 for levonorgestrel-containing OCs).

Idiopathic VTE may rarely be a sign of malignancy or thrombophilia. A study of 26,653 Danish patients with idiopathic VTE found that 1 in 146 had malignancy and 40% were metastatic at the time of diagnosis. Malignancy is more common when idiopathic VTE is recurrent (up to 17%).

In one study, the overall rate of DVT associated with PICC lines was 3%. However, the rate in patients with cancer and those in the ICU was higher (6.7% and 13.9% respectively). However, there was no increase in the risk of developing a PE.
In a study of 2584 patients with syncope and no clear cause, 560 were admitted to the hospital, of whom 97 had a PE (17.3% of hospitalized patients, less than 4% of the entire group).
Hospitalized patients with COVID-19 appear to have an increased risk of thrombotic events including VTE, stroke, and coronary events. See "Primary Prevention."
NSAIDs increase the risk very slightly (0.004%) in women, and a bit more when taken with hormonal contraceptives.

Vascular endothelial damage promotes platelet adhesion resulting in a hemostatic plug, which activates the coagulation pathway. PE results when there is vascular endothelial injury, stasis of blood flow, or hypercoagulation of blood (Virchow's triad) that cause more coagulants to accumulate than usual.
In more than 90% of cases of PE, the thrombus originates in the deep veins of the lower extremities.
Only approximately 10% of emboli cause pulmonary infarction. Most PEs are multiple and usually involve the lower lobes.

Impaired oxygenation is the result of an obstructed vascular bed (altered V/Q ratio) and release of inflammatory mediators (intrapulmonary shunting). Right ventricular failure occurs when approximately 75% of the vascular bed is occluded.
The hemodynamic consequences of PE are directly related to the size and number of emboli, as well as to the preexisting cardiac and respiratory status.

Acquired and inherited thrombophilias that affect the coagulation or anticoagulation cascade can lead to a hypercoagulable state. Some of these disorders include Factor V Leiden mutation, G2021A mutation, protein C and S and antithrombin III deficiencies, hyperhomocysteinemia and antiphosphliid antibody syndrome.

Bed rest for more than 3 days
Immobility due to sitting (eg, prolonged car or air travel)

list.listitem: Each medical and surgical inpatient should be assessed for their individual risk of developing VTE and treated appropriately (). A

In patients with unprovoked VTE, extended anticoagulant therapy (particularly warfain) has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence of VTE, as has aspirin (although to a lesser extent). Extended therapy should therefore be considered in selected patients after a careful assessment of risks and benefits.A
Screening for asymptomatic VTE should not be done routinely since it is not cost-effective and has not been demonstrated to improve outcomes. A

For hospitalized patients who are positive for current COVID-19 infection, prophylactic doses of low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) should be considered in all patients (both critical and non-critical) unless contraindicated by acute bleeding risk.B
Routine screening for asymptomatic DVT using ultrasonography is not effective in patients with hip or knee replacements and is not recommended.

While family members of persons with an episode of VTE and a thrombophilia such as Factor V Leiden are at an increased risk of the mutation and therefore VTE, the risk is small and genetic testing is not recommended.

Since current thrombophilia testing is insufficient to identify inherited risks of VTE and absolute VTE risk is only mildly influenced by these disorders, current recommendations are to not test the majority of patients and to simply utilize their personal and family history to identify their risk.
VTE prophylaxis will reduce the incidence of DVT during the postoperative period by 67% and will prevent death from PE in 1 patient of every 200 undergoing a major operation.
For outpatients with lower limb immobilization, a Cochrane review concluded that LMWH effectively reduces the risk of DVT.
Surgical prophylaxis is ideally started before or shortly after surgery and continued until the patient is fully ambulatory.
Consider primary prophylaxis on the basis of an individual's thromboembolic risk (see ).

In medical inpatients, a meta-analysis concluded that 5000 units unfractionated heparin 2 to 3 times daily will prevent 1 PE and 2 DVTs per 1000 patient days, but will cause 1 major bleed for every 2500 patient days. A Cochrane review drew generally similar conclusions, although found no evidence that prophylaxis reduces the likelihood of PE (only DVT).

There is a high risk of PE among inpatients with COVID-19; in a series of 3334 patients rates of pulmonary embolism were 6.2% in the ICU and 2.2% on the ward. Prophylactic anticoagulation is recommended for hospitalized patients with COVID-19. Recommendations from the American Society of Hematology, though of low certainty, are in favor of prophylactic-intensity anticoagulation over intermediate-intensity or therapeutic-intensity anticoagulation for patients with COVID-19–related critical illness or acute illness who do not have confirmed or suspected VTE.

Similarly, CHEST guidelines (2019, updated 2022) recommend standard dose therapeutic anticoagulation for hospitalized patients with COVID-19 at low risk of bleeding with UFH or LMWH over thromboprophylactic dosing. For patients at higher risk of bleeding consider thromboprophylactic dosing with UFH or LMWH. Antiplatelet agents are not recommended. Screening for asymptomatic VTE is not recommended. The guidelines do not recommend continuing anticoagulation in these patients post-discharge.

However, a Brazilian trial of hospitalized COVID-19 patients at increase risk for VTE and an elevated d-dimer at discharge, rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for 35 days post-discharge reduced the likelihood of symptomatic VTE and fatal VTE (0.6% vs 5.0%, RR 0.13, 95% CI 0.02-0.99, NNT = 23).

In a drug company sponsored RCT comparing oral rivaroxaban with subcutaneous enoxaparin, there were fewer combined DVTs, PEs or death (absolute risk reduction 3.19%; 95% CI, 0.71-5.67; p = 0.0118) but more major bleeds (0.7% vs. 0.3%). Similar benefit was found in two other studies of prophylaxis after total knee and hip arthroplasty, with no significant difference in bleeding.

Rivaroxaban was more effective than enoxaparin in the prevention of VTE events (including PE) during periods of immobilization after non-major orthopedic surgery of the lower limbs and did not confer an increased bleeding risk compared to enoxaparin.

Aspirin has not been shown to be beneficial for VTE prophylaxis in hospitalized patients. However, a study of 1718 patients who had undergone joint replacement and received 5 days of rivaroxaban in hospital found that after discharge, rates of bleeding and VTE were similar whether patients were randomized to 90 days of aspirin or 90 days of rivaroxaban.

A randomized trial with 5416 patients showed superiority of enoxaparin over aspirin for VTE prophylaxis following THA or TKA. Symptomatic VTE occurred more often in the aspirin group (3.45% vs 1.82%, p < 0.05, NNT = 59).

listitem.strong: Compression stockings and pneumatic leg compression

list.listitem: The evidence regarding compression stockings and pneumatic leg compression is mixed. One large trial randomized 1858 inpatients undergoing elective surgery with moderate or high risk of VTE to LMHW + compression stockings versus LMWH alone. Most of the surgeries were gastrointestingal or gynecologic. The risk of VTE was 1.7% with LMWH alone and 1.4% with the combination (non-inferior).

In a meta-analysis of 70 trials enrolling 16,164 patients, intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) was more effective than doing nothing in preventing PE (RR 0.48) and DVT (RR 0.43); and was superior to thromboembolic deterrent stockings (TEDS) in preventing DVT (RR 0.61) but not PE. Compared to LMWH or low dose unfractionated heparin, IPC use was associated with less systemic bleeding (RR 0.41) and similar rates of DVT and PE.

A Cochrane review of 34 RCTs found a greater benefit to intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) + pharmacological prophylaxis to pharmacological prophylaxis alone (0.91% vs 1.84%, OR 0.46, 95% CI 0.30-0.71, NNT = 107).
In another study, thigh-length graduated compression stockings did not reduce the risk of deep vein thrombosis after stroke.

A Cochrane review concluded that use of combined intermittent pneumatic leg compression and pharmacological prophylaxis vs. monotherapy in high risk patients reduces the incidence of both symptomatic pulmonary embolism (PE) (from about 3% to 1%; OR 0.39; 95% CI, 0.25-0.63) and deep vein thrombosis (DVT) (from about 4% to 1%; OR 0.43; 95% CI, 0.24-0.76).

While there is good evidence that graduated compression stockings (GCS) are effective at reducing the risk of DVT in hospitalized patients who have undergone general or orthopedic surgeries, there is only low-quality evidence that GCS reduces the risk of PE in these patients.
Rivaroxaban 10 mg orally once daily was found to be effective and safe for thromboprophylaxis after bariatric surgery.

A meta-analysis of individual patient data from two trials found that in patients with a first unprovoked episode of DVT or PE, after the period of anticoagulation was over, aspirin reduced the likelihood of recurrence compared with placebo (NNT = 33 per year) with no increased risk of bleeding, but less so than anticoagulation (32% vs. 60%-90%).

One trial found that a low-molecular-weight heparin was safer and more effective in reducing recurrent thromboembolism than oral anticoagulation with warfarin for secondary prophylaxis of VTE in patients with cancer. The number needed to treat is 13 to prevent 1 recurrent episode of VTE. However, a second RCT found no difference in outcomes between tinzaparin and warfarin as secondary prevention for recurrent pulmonary embolism in patients with VTE.
Consider indefinite treatment with warfarin for patients who have a high-risk thrombophilia or who experience recurrent idiopathic VTE ().
It is unknown whether vena cava filters are useful in for the prevention of most PE.

A meta-analysis of 15 observational studies with 232 patients (low quality of evidence) found that inferior vena cava filter placement was associated with low recurrent PE and PE-related mortality rates among patients with massive and submassive PE, suggesting of a potential clinical benefit in this scenario.
A Cochrane review concluded that compression stockings reduce the likelihood of postthrombotic syndrome.

A single trial randomized 617 adults with an initial episode of unprovoked DVT or PE to the glycosaminoglycan sulodexide. After 2 years, there were fewer episodes of recurrent venous thromboembolism in the treatment group (4.9% vs. 9.7%; p = 0.02; NNT = 20) and no difference in bleeding.

A study identified 671 patients with cancer and recent VTE and randomized them to a DOAC or LMWH. Recurrent VTE was less likely with DOAC (6.1% vs 8.8%, NNT = 37). Major bleeding was similar between groups and those in the DOAC group had better adherence.
Diagnostic assessment should begin with an assessment of the patient's likelihood of PE using a validated clinical decision rule (). A
The combination of clinical probability and the results of one or more diagnostic tests allows the physician to differentiate PE from other conditions with confidence in most patients (see ). A
CT-PA and V/Q scan are both options for imaging in patients with suspected PE and an abnormal age-adjusted D dimer. B

list.listitem: Dyspnea, tachypnea, or pleuritic chest pain is present in 97% of patients. Sudden onset of dyspnea is the best individual predictor of PE, while gradual onset reduces the likelihood. Syncope or shock is the hallmark of massive PE, but may occur in patients with a smaller PE.

The diagnosis of PE on the basis of clinical signs and symptoms is difficult since its presentation is highly variable (from subclinical to shock). No single clinical feature can effectively rule it in or rule it out. Clinical assessment is more accurate by more experienced clinicians. High probability clinical assessment has a positive likelihood ratio of 5.7, compared with 0.3 for low probability assessment.

While one should consider PE in older patients presenting with unexplained syncope, it is uncommon. One Italian series found that 4% of such patients (including 17% of those sick enough to be hospitalized) had PE as the cause of their syncope. However, a large study using administrative databases in Canada, Italy, Denmark and the US found that PE was diagnosed in less than 0.55% of patients, and even in those hospitalized for syncope, only 1% to 2% had pulmonary embolism. A systematic review of 12 studies with 7583 patients found a rate of pulmonary embolism of only 1.8%, even when including the Italian study in the mix.
If present, syncope is associated with higher mortality (OR 1.82; CI, 1.14 to 2.90) and higher prevalence of hemodynamic instability (OR 4.36; CI, 2.27 to 8.37) in those with PE.
ECG, CXR, and arterial blood gas are not sensitive or specific enough to diagnose or exclude PE by themselves but can be helpful to identify alternative diagnoses.

The diagnosis of PE requires a combination of a pretest probability estimate using a clinical decision rule (i.e. Wells or Geneva criteria),D-dimer, and for many patients CT pulmonary angiography (CT-PA) or V/Q scan. See algorithm in . A randomized controlled trial found that CT-PA was not inferior to V/Q scanning in ruling out PE, but 30% more patients were diagnosed with PE using the CT-PA approach. The thromboembolic complications and observed mortality in the two groups were similar.

In patients with a low likelihood assessed by clinical rule, PE is excluded by a negative D-dimer. When clinical probability is moderate to high, PE is confirmed by a high probability lung scan or a positive CT-PA and ruled out by a normal V/Q scan or CT-PA. If the V/Q scan or CT-PA are indeterminate, further testing is necessary. ACP guidelines recommend CT-PA as the preferred test for most patients.

An age-adjusted d-dimer cutoff is calculated as follows: the cutoff is 500 mcg/L for patients 50 and under, and is 10x the age for those over age 50 years. A study found that the age adjusted d-dimer was safe and could rule out PE in more patients when used in conjunction with the Wells rule.

A systematic review and meta-analysis examining the diagnostic accuracy of D-dimer tests for PE in patients with COVID-19 concluded that the usual cutoffs for D-dimer levels seem applicable to patients with COVID-19.

In fact, ACP guidelines recommend that low risk patients who meet all of the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria should not have either d-dimer or imaging (they have <1% chance of developing a PE in 30 days). However, those who are positive for any of the PERC criteria, just like those deemed intermediate probability for PE, should have a d-dimer.

In a prospective study of 3324 patients presenting to the ED with a clinical suspicion of PE (but with a low low pretest probability of PE based upon Geneva or Wells scores), using an age adjusted cut-off for D-dimer testing (ie, in patients over the age of 50 the age-adjusted level was defined as age x 10 mcg/L) resulted in fewer false-positive tests. Approximately 12% of patients had D-dimer values between 500 and their age adjusted cutoff and were not treated and after 3 months of follow up only 1 in 331 (0.3%) was determined to have a PE. Using the age adjusted cutoff in patients over the age of 75, increased the true-negative rate to 29.7% (compared to 6.4% using the traditional cutoff of 500) without additional false negative tests. A European study had similar findings, with the age-adjusted cutoff identifying a larger percentage of patients (42% vs. 36%) in whom PE could be ruled out. ACP guidelines recommend using the age-adjusted d-dimer thresholds for patients older than 50 years (age x 10 ng/ml).

The Pulmonary Embolism Graduated D-Dimer (PEGeD) strategy can be used to rule out lower risk patients with suspected PE just using clinical pretest probability and d-dimer levels without the need for imaging studies. The greatest benefit is seen in patients with low prestest probability and a didimer between 500 ng/mL and 999 ng/mL. This increased d-dimer threshold (< 1000 ng/mL instead of 500 ng/mL) in patients with low clinical probability decreased chest imaging from 51.9% to 34.3%.

Choice of CT-PA versus V/Q scan depends on local expertise and availability. CT-PA is preferred over the V/Q scan if the chest x-ray is abnormal. It may not be sufficiently sensitive to exclude PE in patients with relatively high pretest probability. On the other hand, V/Q scans are diagnostic in only approximately one third of patients. Single-photon emission CT lung scintigraphy ("SPECT V/Q scintigraphy") is an accurate alternative to CT pulmonary angiography, with similar accuracy.

Pulmonary angiography is indicated when the probability of PE is moderate or high but the V/Q or CT-PA results are neither diagnostic (high probability) nor normal and the lower extremity Doppler studies are negative. It should also be considered when the risk of complications of treatment is high.

A prospective study with 274 participants compared use of subtraction CT versus dual-energy CT iodine maps to CT angiography for detecting PE. Use of subtraction CT iodine maps (a software-only solution) had a greater specificity than CT angiography alone in PE detection and was comparable to dual-energy CT, without the need for dedicated hardware.

Echocardiography should be performed in patients with suspected massive PE to confirm right ventricular overload and dysfunction. It is also helpful in distinguishing alternative diagnoses, such as endocarditis, pericardial tamponade, and aortic dissection.

In patients with PE who have echocardiographic studies performed, an enlarged right ventricle and atrium along with peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity are all independent predictors of mortality in PE patients, with an exponential increase in mortality when all 3 parameters are elevated.

In patients suspected to have a PE presenting with tachycardia (pulse > 99 beats/min or hypotension (systolic blood pressure <90 mm/Hg), a negative echocardiographic FOCUS exam (assessment for right ventricular dilation, McConnell's sign, septal flattening, tricuspid regurgitation, and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion) significantly lowered the likelihood of a PE diagnosis (92% sensitivity, 64% specificity, LR- 0.12).
In patients with unprovoked VTE, routine CT scans to detect occult malignancy were not helpful in a randomized trial of 1716 patients.
A systematic review of 10 studies with 590 patients concluded that CT and MRI had similar accuracy (90% sens/88% spec for CT, 92% sens/91% spec for MRI).

ACP guidelines recommend that a validated clinical prediction rule should be used to estimate the pretest probability of PE, which can then be used as the basis for the interpretation of subsequent tests.

The most widely used clinical decision rule for diagnosis of PE is the Wells rule. It has been prospectively validated in a variety of settings and does not require laboratory or imaging studies. See .
However, one retrospective study found that while a Wells score >4 was associated with the presence of PE in patients with COVID-19, the sensitivity and overall accuracy were poor (AUC 0.54).

Alternate rules that have also been prospectively validated include the Geneva and Pisa scores. However, both require ECG, chest x-ray and/or blood gas results limiting their applicability to the emergency department setting.

The Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria (PERC) can be used in those patients already determined to be low risk by clinical decision rules to further determine if someone is at low enough risk that they require no further evaluation. It should not be used in those patients who are at intermediate or high risk, and it is not intended to be used to risk-stratify patients as other clinical decision rules do.

Use well-validated clinical scores like the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI) or simplified-PESI (s-PESI) to provide objective measures of the patient's risk for complications, as well as their appropriateness for outpatient management and hospital discharge. Both clinical scores help to identify those patients who are at low 30-day mortality risk based on the patient's baseline indicators of PE and their potential aggrevating conditions and comorbidities.
The eStiMaTe calculator is based on a registry with over 62,000 patients with PE. It uses a version of PESI plus several biomarkers to estimate 30 day risk of mortality and complications.
A validated clinical risk score can identify patients at high risk of VTE events within the 90 days following surgery.
The prognosis (30-day mortality) for patients with acute pulmonary embolism and cancer can be estimated using a validated risk score.

A study compared the YEARS rule aided by d-dimer with the Wells rule and found that the YEARS rule was somewhat better at reducing the need for CT angiography in patients with suspected PE (48% vs. 34% not needing the study).

The YEARS algorithm provides a simplified method to evaluate patients suspected of having PE with a two tiered system incorporating different d-dimer thresholds. Items include any clinical signs of DVT, hemoptysis, and PE being the most likely diagnosis. Based on the response, if any item is positive, a 500 ng/mL d-dimer threshold should be used to decide if a CTPA is warranted. The d-dimer threshold increases to 1000 ng/mL if all items are negative.
The YEARS algorithm has been validated for use in pregnant patients and reduces the number of potential CT scans by up to 40%.

Regarding recurrence of VTE and PE, the Leiden Thrombosis Recuurrence Risk Prediction Model (L-TRRiP) can be used to predict risk of VTE recurrence. In one population-based case control study using 5000 adults with either DVT or PE, using internal and external validation methods, along with a mean follow up period of 5.7 years, authors were able to demonstrate that a combination of clinical risk factors along with laboratory paramaters could predict future VTE events.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to evaluation.

Another approach has been prospectively validated in a randomized trial of 1414 patients with clinically suspected PE and a PERC score greater than 0. If they had none of the YEARS criteria (PE is the most likely diagnosis, hemoptysis, and/or clinical sign of DVT) and their d-dimer was < 1000 ng/ml, they were considered ruled out. If they had 1 or more YEARS criteria, but their d-dimer was less than the age-adjusted d-dimer cutoff (500 for ages 0 to 50, and age x 10 if age greater than 50 years), PE was excluded. This was non-inferior to an algorithm just using a d-dimer cutoff of 500 alone in terms of missed PEs (0.15% vs 0.80% in the control group). Use of chest imaging was lower (30% vs 40%) and ED stay was shorter.
Unless clinical suspicion is low or bleeding risk is high, initiate empiric treatment for PE before the full diagnostic evaluation has been completed. B
A direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivvaroxaban, dabigatran, or edoxaban) is the preferred initial anticoagulant per 2021 ACCP guidelines.A
Duration of treatment varies according to the underlying cause and risk factors (). A
Consider surveillance only for patients with subsegmental PE, no lower extremity DVT, and no increased risk for recurrence.B
Extended anticoagulation is recommended for patients with unprovoked PE and a low or moderate risk of bleeding complications.B
ACCP guidelines (2021) describe three phases of therapy: initiation phase, a treatment phase for 3 months, and an extended phase for selected patients.

ACCP guidelines (2021) recommend that for patients with subsegmental PE, no proximal DVT in the legs, and who are at low risk for recurrent VTE, clinical observation without anticoagulation is recommended.

A subsequent study found that 3.1% of 292 patients with one or more subsegmental PEs had a recurrence within 90 days (there were no deaths). The incidence of recurrent VTE was higher with multiple subsegmental PEs than with a single subsegmental PE (5.7% vs 2.1%). Additionally, patients older than 65 years had a higher incidence than younger patients (5.5% vs 1.8%).

ACCP guidelines (2021) recommend outpatient therapy for PE if patients are clinically stable; there is no recent bleeding, thrombocytopenia, or severe liver or kidney disease; and they feel well enough to be treated at home and are likely to be adherent.

An individual patient data meta-analysis of 10 studies with 2694 patients discharged within 24 hours and treated at home found 14 day mortality of 0.11% and 30 day mortality of 0.30%. Patients with cancer had an association with higher 30 day mortality (RR 4.9, 95% CI 2.7 to 9.1). Cancer, elevated troponin, and elevated NT-proBNP were associated with an increased likelihood of adverse events.
For patients with asymptomatic PE incidentally diagnosed during CT of the chest, anticoagulation is still recommended as studies have shown a similar prognosis to symptomatic PE.

All patients with suspected PE who have no contraindication to anticoagulation should be started on low-molecular-weight heparin or unfractionated heparin immediately. Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is at least as safe as unfractionated heparin for the treatment of PE (except in renal failure and massive PE). It may also be associated with lower mortality, less risk of bleeding, and may be more cost-effective than unfractionated heparin.

If unfractionated heparin is used, therapeutic levels (aPTT 1.5-2.5 times normal) must be achieved within 24 hours. Fixed-dose subcutaneous unfractionated heparin (333 U/kg initially, followed by 250 U/kg every 12 hours) was similarly effective to low-molecular-weight heparin in one study of 708 patients, 19% of whom had PE.

If warfarin is used for long term anticoagulation, it should be started at the same time as heparin. Clinical rules based on 5 and 10 mg protocols have been developed to guide initiation of warfarin therapy and more quickly achieve therapeutic levels. Heparin may be discontinued when the INR is between 2.0 and 3.0 for at least 2 consecutive days.
Idraparinux was not as effective as heparin for PE treatment. Oral ximelagatran was as effective as enoxaparin followed by warfarin in patients with PE.

Most major guidelines (American College of Chest Physicians, European Sociatey of Cardiology, and American Society of Hematology) indicate that direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, edoxaban, dabigatran, or rivaroxaban) are the preferred first-line anticoagulant therapy in most patients.
The ACCP guidelines (2021) recommend that an exception should be made for patients with antiphospholipid syndrome, for whom warfarin is recommended during the treatment phase.
Dabigatran in a fixed-dose regimen after initial overlap with LMWH, was as effective as warfarin in the treatment of VTE with a similar safety profile.

Oral rivaroxaban (15 milligrams twice daily for three weeks followed by 20 milligrams once daily) was non-inferior to standard therapy (enoxaparin followed by warfarin or acenocoumarol) for up to 12 months in preventing recurrent VTE (50 events vs. 44 events), but was associated with a slightly lower risk of major bleeding (1.1% vs. 2.2%; NNT = 90).
Edoxaban (a newer oral Xa inhibitor) is non-inferior to warfarin regarding safety and efficacy in treating patients with acute venous thromboembolism (VTE).
Apixaban in a fixed-dose regimen alone was shown non-inferior to LMWH followed by warfarin for the treatment of acute VTE and also associated with significantly less bleeding.
DOACs are non-inferior to LMWH (and long-term warfarin treatment) for recurrent VTE and have a lower bleeding risk.
DOACs also show good tolerability in the elderly with apixaban considered the most appropriate DOAC when assessed in several studies.

Recent randomized-controlled trials (Hokusai-VTE Cancer, SELECT-D, & CARAVAGGIO) also show that the DOACs edoxaban, rivaroxaban and apixaban are non-inferior to LMWH in the treatment of patients with VTE and concurrent cancer. The American Society of Hematology recommends LMWH or DOACs in ambulatory patients with cancer receiving systemic therapy at high risk of VTE and either LMWH or DOAC for initial treatment of VTE in patients with cancer.

Adding pharmacogenetic information to otherwise well-validated algorithms for warfarin dosing adds no benefit, and may be associated with less time spent in the therapeutic range in patients of African-American descent.

For patients with simultaneous PE and cerebral infarct, assess risks and benefits but do consider anticoagulation. If there is evidence of hemorrhage, consider IVC filter insertion and delayed anticoagulation.

In a study of patients who experienced an initial, unprovoked (idiopathic) deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, they were randomized to aspirin 100 mg per day after their course of anticoagulation (initial treatment between 6 and 18 months) or placebo. The rate of recurrent VTE was 6.6% in the aspirin group vs. 11.2% in the placebo group (NNT = 22 over 2 years of treatment). This was confirmed in an individual patient meta-analysis of two similar trials.
ACCP guidelines (2021) recommend daily low dose aspirin following cessation of extended phase anticoagulation.

A randomized trial of patients with VTE compared extended anticoagulation with aspirin versus rivaroxaban found lower risks of recurrent VTE with rivaroxaban (NNT = 33) over 12 months of extended anticoagulation. Rates of major bleeding were similar.
The treatment table within the DVT topic provides a useful overview on treatment and prophylaxis options.

Surgical embolectomy or catheter-assisted extraction of massive PE should be considered in patients with massive PE and refractory shock and when anticoagulation or thrombolysis have failed or are contraindicated. This includes patients within 1 week of surgery at increased risk of bleeding complications.

Large-bore mechanical thrombectomy (LBMT) and catheter directed thrombolysis (CDT) are options for patients with intermediate or high risk PE who are clinically unstable or deteriorating. A trial randomized 550 patients with acute intermediate risk PE (right ventricular dilatation or dysfunction, a proximal filling defect in at least one main or lobar pulmonary artery, and signs of clinical instability based on vital signs) LBMT or CDT. The LBMT group was less likely to experience clinical deterioration (1.8% vs 5.4%, p = 0.04, NNT = 28) and less need for ICU care (42% vs 98%, p < 0.001, NNT = 2). There was no difference between groups in major bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, or mortality.

Inferior vena cava filter placement should be considered if anticoagulation is contraindicated, in patients with recurrent PE despite adequate anticoagulation, or if severe bleeding complications occur during anticoagulation. Inferior vena cava filter placement decreases initial PE risk, but increases long-term recurrent DVT risk almost 2-fold without conferring any long-term recurrence or mortality benefit.
In an RCT, adding a temporary inferior vena cava filter to anticoagulation for patients at high risk of recurrence or with poor cardiopulmonary reserve did not provide any additional benefit.
Additionally, early prophylactic placement of vena cava filters after major trauma did not lower the risk of symptomatic PE or 90 day mortality when compared to no filter placement.
Initial care of the patient with acute PE should focus on stabilizing the patient with respiratory and hemodynamic support when necessary.
In patients who have coexistent right ventricular dysfunction, give IV fluids cautiously since they can precipitate right ventricular failure.
Thrombolytic therapy has been shown to be effective if applied within the first 48 hours of symptom onset. However efficacy decreases significantly after 7 days

Ultrasound-assisted catheter directed thrombolysis has been shown to be both safe and effective in the treatment of acute massive or submassive PEs and is associated with significant hemodynamic and clinical improvement.

Consider thrombolysis in patients with high-risk PE with otherwise unexplainable shock and/or persistent hypotension, pulmonary hypertension or right heart failure, or if anticoagulation has been unsuccessful in hemodynamically unstable patients. While it may decrease mortality in high risk patients, it also increases the risk of major bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage significantly. Thrombolysis could also be considered in patients who are high risk based on their Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI) score, and who have elevated troponin and lower limb DVT present. present but low bleeding risk.

An RCT compared fibrinolytic therapy with tenecteplase vs. placebo in patients who were hemodynamically stable but were at intermediate risk for adverse outcomes based on right ventricular dysfunction or myocardial injury. They found no difference in mortality, and a small decrease in the likelihood of hemodynamic compensation. However, harms included major bleeding (NNH = 11) and hemorrhagic stroke (NNH = 55).

Usual dosing for alteplase in patients over 65 kg is 10 mg bolus over 1 to 2 minutes followed by a 90 mg infusion. If patients are under 65 kg, the total dose administered (including the 10 mg bolus) should be 1.5 mg/kg.
Duration of therapy depends on patient characteristics (). The first episode of idiopathic PE should be treated for at least 6 months.

ACCP guidelines (2021) recommend extended anticoagulation for patients with an unprovoked PE and low or moderate bleeding risk. If high bleeding risk, 3 months of anticoagulation are recommended. The same is true in the event of a second unprovoked PE. During the extended phase, a lower dose is recommended, either apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily or rivaroxaban 10 mg once daily.

A study randomized 600 patients with unprovoked VTE but at least one ongoing risk factors (BMI > 30, chronic inflammatory disease or chronic lung disease) to 3 versus 12 months of apixaban. The likelihood of symptomatic recurrent VTE was significantly lower in the apixaban group (1.3% vs 10.0%; P < .001; number needed to treat [NNT] = 11). There were reductions in both DVT (4 vs 23) and PE (0 vs 11) in the apixaban group. With regard to harm, major bleeding occurred in 1 patient in the apixaban group and none in the placebo group; clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was numerically more common with apixaban (4.8% vs 1.7%; P = .06).

A study of 178 patients with active cancer and a "low-risk" PE randomized them to 6 vs 18 months of DOAC. There were fewer thrombi detected in the 18 month group (5.6% vs 19.1%, p = 0.01, NNT = 7) but the all but 4 (all in the 6 month group) were asymptomatic. All-cause mortality was numerically higher in the 18-month group, but this difference was not statistically significant (32.6% vs 25.8%).

In patients with idiopathic VTE, an abnormal D-dimer 30 days after the end of treatment predicts a greater likelihood of recurrent VTE. These patients should consider extended, or even indefinite, anticoagulation.

A randomized trial comparing 6 months with 18 months of anticoagulation with warfarin for an unprovoked PE found a lower likelihood of symptomatic recurrent VTE in the 18 month group (NNT = 9) and a small increase in the risk of major bleeding (NNH = 61).

A recent systematic review and meta-analysis also supported extended anticoagulation (6 months to 2 years) for patients with unprovoked VTE, especially PE. The net clinical benefit that incorporated recurrent VTE and major bleeding was reduced for both warfarin treatment (NNT=16) and direct oral anticoagulants (NNT = 15).

Another recent systematic review and meta-analysis showed that 1 in 10 patients can expect to have a second VTE within a year after finishing anticoagulation therapy, and 40% will have a second VTE over 10 years.
In all instances, longer duration of anticoagulation should be considered and weighed against the bleeding risk.
When extending therapy with apixaban or rivaroxaban to longer than 6 months, current recommendations are to use prophylactic doses (2.5 mg twice per day for apixaban and 10mg daily for rivaroxaban).

Consider consultation with a coagulation specialist for patients with recurrent VTE, if alternative anticoagulants are being considered, if there is an increased risk of bleeding, and for pregnant women.
Any patient with cardiovascular or respiratory compromise should be admitted to the intensive care unit.

Outpatient initial management may be appropriate in low-risk patients (see PESI score above) including those with good cardiorespiratory reserve, no excessive bleeding risks, a creatinine clearance greater than 30 mL/min, and ability to safely self-administer the medication.
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia occurs in 0.1% to 1.0% of medical patients. It occurs with equal frequency in patients using unfractionated heparin and low-molecular-weight heparin.
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is treated with prompt discontinuation of heparin. Anticoagulation can be continued with a direct thrombin inhibitor or with fondaparinux.
There is some evidence that intermittent pneumatic compression units are successful for the treatment of postthrombotic syndrome.

The postthrombotic syndrome occurs in almost one third of patients (cumulative incidence = 30% after 8 years).

The eStiMaTe calculator is based on a registry with over 62,000 patients with PE. It uses a version of PESI plus several biomarkers to estimate 30 day risk of mortality and complications.

Right ventricular dysfunction on echocardiogram is associated with a 2-fold increase in PE-related mortality. Hypotension, elevated troponin, elevated Factor VIII levels, and elevated brain-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels are all predictors of worse outcome.
Early mortality after VTE is also strongly associated with presentation as PE (as opposed to DVT), advanced age, and comorbid cancer or cardiovascular disease.

Complete resolution of PE takes place in 13% of patients 1 week after occurrence, and in 50% of patients after 11 months. Overall, more than 50% of patients have persistent defects on follow-up scan 6 months after diagnosis.

Initiation of appropriate therapy decreases the incidence of fatal PE to less than 1% except in patients with idiopathic disease, those with cancer, and in those with prothrombotic biochemical abnormalities.
Approximately 5% of treated patients with PE develop pulmonary hypertension as a result of poor resolution.
For patients with underlying cancer, a validated risk score can be used to predict 30-day mortality.
The patient's INR should be maintained between 2.0 and 3.0. The duration of anticoagulation depends on the clinical setting in which the PE occurred and any associated comorbidities (see ).
A normal D-dimer level 1 month after discontinuation of anticoagulation is associated with a lower risk of recurrence (3.7% vs. 11.5%).
An echocardiogram showing right ventricular dysfunction at the time of discharge also predicts recurrent VTE.

Patients taking anticoagulation should be informed about: the signs and symptoms of bleeding; avoiding harmful situations which could lead to significant bleeding; being aware of drug-drug interactions before starting a new medication; and the importance of compliance and laboratory monitoring.
Pregnant women have a 5-fold increased risk for VTE.

Prevention and management of VTE associated with pregnancy must consider outcomes of both mother and fetus, and treatment decisions should account for baseline and pregnancy-specific clinical factors and patient preferences.

Pregnant women with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) have an even higher risk for VTE (mainly DVT) when compared to pregnant women without VTE in both pregnancy (RR 2.13 [CI 1.66-2.73]) and post-partum periods (RR 2.61 [CI 1.84-3.69]). The risk was higher in those patients with ulcerative colitis than in those with Crohn's disease.
In a study of 149 pregnant women, a D-dimer test (SimpliRED) identified all 13 women with DVT and had 60% specificity, similar to its performance in nonpregnant women.
The YEARS algorithm, adapted for pregnancy, safely identifies approximately 40% of women who are clinically suspected of having PE as not requiring CT imaging.

There is insufficient evidence to make specific recommendations for types of anticoagulation regimens for VTE in pregnant women. Subcutaneous low-dose unfractionated heparin is the prophylactic regimen of choice for pregnant women at high risk for VTE, although data on efficacy from controlled trials are lacking.

Regarding prophylaxis during pregnancy, a Cochrane review found only limited comparisons between LMWH and UFH, and no comparisons of external compression stockings or devices with anticoagulants in pregnant or recently pregnant women.

Warfarin should not be used because it crosses the placenta causing embryopathy and fetal bleeding. Low-molecular-weight heparin does not cross the placenta, and is the drug of choice for women with non-massive pulmonary embolism requiring treatment. Long-term therapy with low-molecular-weight heparin may be considered in pregnant women with malignancy.

PE is very rare in children. A review recommends CT as first-line choice for imaging, but notes that MRI is emerging as a good choice given the lack of ionizing radiation and greater sensitivity of children to radiation.

A study identified persons younger than 18 years who have VTE due to a provoking factor (e.g. hospitalization, trauma, central venous catheterization), evidence of venous flow at 6 weeks, and no antiphospholipid antibodies at 6 weeks. They were randomized to stopping anticoagulation at 6 weeks or continuing for an additional 6 weeks. The shorter duration was non-inferior, with 6 weeks of therapy resulting in (nonsignificantly) less recurrence of VTE and less incidence of clinically relevant bleeding.

feature.caption: Levels of Thromboembolism Risk and Recommended Prophylaxis.
feature.feature_body:
Level of Risk Definition Prevention Strategies Comment
Surgical patients
Low Minor surgery* Early ambulation All patients should be reassessed for risk every 3 days
Younger than 40 years
No risk factors**
Moderate Minor surgery in patients with risk factors UFH 5000 U every 12 hours, OR Continue until patient fully ambulatory
Major surgery* in patients aged 40-60 years with no risk factors (especially cardiothoracic) Enoxaparin 30 mg subcutaneously daily (not if serum creatinine >2 mg/dL, OR Order platelet count every day on all patients taking UFH or LMWH
Intermittent pneumatic compression
High Older than 60 years UFH 5,000 U every 8 hours, OR Start as close to time of surgery as possible
Aged 40-60 years with risk factors Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily (not if serum creatinine >2 mg/dL, OR Continue until patient fully ambulatory
